findings.description: The change calls `env.canReferenceType(ref)` and `env.canReferenceType(pipeRef)` on `ReferenceEmitEnvironment`, but the diff does not add that method. It also removes `checkIfClassIsExported` without adding a replacement in the shown files. If the method is absent, this fails to compile. If it is added elsewhere, the diff is incomplete and the exported check cannot be verified. The new test also passes a `{rootDir: '/root'}` option to `diagnose`, and that signature change is not shown either.

The new guard uses the generic `_placeholderRe` (`__ph-N__`), but SafeSelector uses that placeholder for attribute selectors (`[attr=...]`) and `:not(...)` content as well as for escapes. A selector like `a[href] big` or `[type=text] div` therefore has a part ending in a placeholder. If the next character is a hex digit or letter a-f (`b`, `d`, `a`, ...), the descendant-combinator space is treated as part of an escape and skipped. The two compound selectors are then merged and scoped once, so output like `a[href] big[contenta]` is wrong. This is a regression for ordinary selectors. The check should only match placeholders created for backslash escapes. The check also does not verify that the separator is a space, so `.\fc>b` is wrongly skipped too.

The new check treats any part containing a `__ph-N__` placeholder as an escaped hex value. SafeSelector also uses placeholders for attribute selectors (`[attr]`) and `:nth-*(...)` expressions. For a selector such as `[type=text] div`, `a[href] b`, `.x[data-y] a` or `:nth-child(2) em`, the part contains a placeholder and the next character is a hex char (a-f or a digit). The code then skips the descendant-combinator split and the selectors are no longer scoped separately. `[type=text] div` loses the scoping on `div`, and the output has the wrong shape. This regresses scoping for common selectors. The check should confirm that the placeholder is an escape ending in a hex sequence, not merely a placeholder that appears in the part.

The `if (_global.beforeEach)` and `if (_global.afterEach)` guards were removed, so `beforeEach(...)` and `afterEach(...)` now run unconditionally when the module loads. If `@angular/core/testing` is imported where no test framework has defined these globals (a server bundle, a Node script, a non-Jasmine/Mocha/Jest runner), loading the module throws `ReferenceError: beforeEach is not defined`. The old code tolerated this case. A `typeof beforeEach === 'function'` guard is needed.

The previous `if (_global.beforeEach)` and `if (_global.afterEach)` guards were removed, so `beforeEach(...)` and `afterEach(...)` are now called unconditionally at module load. If `@angular/core/testing` is imported where no test framework has defined these globals, such as a non-test context or a runner that does not expose them, the import throws a `ReferenceError`. Before this change it was a silent no-op.

In `collectDeferredSymbols`, `deferBlockDep.isDeferrable` and `importPath` are updated, but `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport` is never set. It stays at its initial `false` from `resolve`. The defer deps functions in `template.ts`, `create_defer_deps_fns.ts` and `compiler.ts` read `dep.isDefaultImport` from the defer block dependency. For a default-imported component they therefore still emit `m => m.CmpA` instead of `m => m.default`, so the dynamic import resolves to `undefined` at runtime. Only the `deferrableTypes` map, used for `setClassMetadataAsync`, gets the correct flag. The new tests that expect `m.default` in the `TestCmp_Defer_1_DepsFn` would fail.

isDefaultImport() only returns true when the import clause has no namedBindings. A mixed import such as `import Foo, {Bar} from './x'` has namedBindings, so it is treated as not default. If the default-imported `Foo` is used in a `@defer` block or in `deferredImports`, the generated loader is `m => m.Foo` instead of `m => m.default`. That resolves to undefined at runtime. The check also does not look at which binding is being deferred, only at the declaration's shape.

The constructor condition is inverted. Previously anchor elements subscribed to navigation events and non-anchor elements got `tabindex=0`. Now `subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary()` runs only when `!isAnchorElement`, where it returns immediately. The `else` branch calls `setTabIndexIfNotOnNativeEl('0')` only for anchor elements, where it is a no-op. As a result, non-anchor hosts such as `<div routerLink>` never get the default `tabindex="0"`, so they are no longer keyboard-focusable. That is an accessibility and behavior regression.

The subscription condition looks wrong. When no `queryParamsHandling` is set and the router's default is `merge` or `preserve`, `createSubcription` stays false, so the link never subscribes to `NavigationEnd`. Its href then goes stale after navigation, because the generated URL depends on the current router state. Conversely, it subscribes when nothing depends on router state. The logic is negated.

The constructor condition is inverted: `if (!this.isAnchorElement) { this.subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary(); } else { this.setTabIndexIfNotOnNativeEl('0'); }`. `subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary` returns early for non-anchor elements, so that call does nothing. The `tabindex="0"` fallback now runs only for anchor elements. Non-anchor hosts such as `<div routerLink>` no longer get a default tabindex and lose keyboard focusability, which is a regression. The condition should be `if (this.isAnchorElement)`.

The subscription condition for the router-state dependency is wrong. It subscribes when `!queryParamsHandling && !dependsOnRouterState(options.defaultQueryParamsHandling)`, meaning when no handling applies, and it skips subscribing when the global default is 'merge' or 'preserve'. With `defaultQueryParamsHandling: 'merge'` and no per-link handling, the href depends on current router state but never updates on NavigationEnd, so it goes stale. The negation on the default should be removed.

The replacement is not equivalent to the old `.toPromise()`. `toPromise()` resolved `undefined` when the source completed without emitting, and it used the last emitted value. `first()` instead rejects with `EmptyError` on an empty-completing source and takes the first value. A `redirectTo` function, `canLoad` guard, or `loadChildren` observable that completes empty used to resolve to `undefined` and now makes navigation fail with `EmptyError`. For `loadChildren`, that bypasses the `if (!cfg) throw canLoadFails(route)` handling.

cancelLeavingNodes cancels any leaving element for the same tNode whose parent differs from the new element's parent. A tNode belongs to the TView, so every instance of a component or template shares it. If instance A's element is playing its leave animation and instance B is inserted into a different parent (for example, two sibling components or list items each with an `animate.leave` element), A's animation is cut short. A's element receives a synthetic cancel `animationend` and is removed from the DOM immediately. The different-parent heuristic cannot tell an overlay re-creation from an unrelated instance, so it breaks leave animations for unrelated elements.

On Detach, the element is now tracked in leavingNodes whenever the tNode has leave animations. That happens even when runLeaveAnimationsWithCallback skips the animation and removes the node immediately, for example when animations are disabled or the element has no actual animation. The entries are only cleared by the leave-animation cleanup, so they can stay in the array indefinitely. The array then holds references to detached DOM elements and grows with each detach. The tracking also runs for every detached node that has leave data, which adds work to a hot path.

The removal of pending enter animations from the queue was dropped when a node with an enter animation is detached. If an element is created and removed before the animation queue flushes, its enter animation function still runs against a node that has already been removed or is leaving. This can start a stray enter animation, or add classes and listeners to the leaving element and interfere with the leave animation.

A TNode is shared by every instance of a template or component, but `cancelLeavingNodes` cancels any leaving element whose parent differs from the new element's parent. For example, two instances of a component each contain `@if (x) { <div animate.leave> }`. Instance 1's div is animating out in parent P1, and instance 2 then inserts the same TNode in parent P2. Instance 1's leave animation is forcibly cancelled and its element removed early, although the two are unrelated. The same happens for `@for` over components or for a template rendered in different containers. This is a regression: leave animations are skipped incorrectly whenever the same TNode is used in different parents.

`trackLeavingNodes` is called on every Detach of a node that has a leave animation, but nothing guarantees `clearLeavingNodes` runs afterwards. This applies when animations are disabled, when the leave function is skipped, or when the leaving node is a descendant that is removed together with its parent. The element then stays in the `leavingNodes` array for that TNode, which leaks DOM nodes. A later insert of the same TNode can also wrongly match a stale element and cancel or remove it.

The removal of queued enter animations for a node that is being detached was dropped, as was the `cancelLeavingNodes` call in the animate instructions. If an element is created and removed before the animation queue flushes, as with rapid toggling, its pending enter animation is no longer discarded. It then runs against a detached or leaving element, which can add stray enter classes or fire listeners and leave state inconsistent.

`position` is an `ElementPosition` (number[]). The old template literal turned it into a comma-separated string such as '0,1,2'. `stringifyAndEscape` now yields the string literal "[0,1,2]", including brackets. The receiving `findConstructorByPosition` does not appear to be updated in this diff; it most likely still parses with `split(',').map(parseInt)`. That would produce NaN for the first and last indices, so View Source would fail to resolve the element or throw.

The same change affects `findDomElementByPosition`. It now receives the string "[0,1,2]" instead of '0,1,2'. If the receiver still splits on commas, the indices are parsed as NaN, so selecting a DOM element from the component tree breaks.

The serialization of `position` changed. Before, `'${position}'` interpolated the array via toString, so the inspected app received a comma-separated string like "0,1,2". Now `stringifyAndEscape(position)` passes the string "[0,1,2]". If `findConstructorByPosition` still parses its input with `split(',')` and `parseInt`, the first and last indices become NaN ("[0" and "2]"). The element lookup then fails and view-source stops working. The receiving side is not updated in this diff. The same applies to `findDomElementByPosition` in `selectDomElement`.
